readerTitle: You'll get bored of your brand long before customers notice it
caseNote: 가상 사례 (비스트로, 프로젝트 관리 앱) + 실제 기업 (De Beers 슬로건)
insight: 브랜드는 고객의 기억 속에 쌓이는 것이고, 고객은 우리가 생각하는 것보다 훨씬 드물게 우리를 본다. 그래서 주인이 지겨워질 때쯤에야 고객은 겨우 기억하기 시작한다.
misconception: 브랜드를 신선하게 유지하려면 메시지, 로고, 분위기를 자주 바꿔야 한다. 같은 걸 오래 쓰면 고객도 지루해한다.

sources.text: De Beers / N.W. Ayer, "A Diamond Is Forever" (Frances Gerety가 1947년 작성, 1948년경부터 사용)
Advertising Age (1999), 20세기 최고의 광고 슬로건 선정
비스트로와 앱 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "A Diamond Is Forever"의 작성 연도(1947)와 첫 사용 시기(1948년경)를 De Beers 또는 광고사 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "since the late 1940s"로만 적었습니다.
Advertising Age가 1999년 이 문구를 20세기 최고의 슬로건으로 선정했다는 내용을 원문으로 확인하세요. 확인되지 않으면 6번 카드에서 해당 문장을 지우세요.
5번 카드의 '주인은 매일, 고객은 1년에 몇 번' 비교는 통계가 아니라 설명용 대비입니다. 구체적 수치를 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: You'll get bored of your brand long before customers notice it
body: Every spring, a neighborhood bistro gets a new look. New name on the menu, new colors, new slogan. The owner calls it staying fresh.
Three years in, she asks regulars to describe the place in one sentence. Most of them can't.

image.label: One bistro front shown in three different seasonal styles
image.brief: 같은 비스트로 외관을 세 칸으로 나란히. 칸마다 간판 색, 글꼴, 차양 무늬가 완전히 다름. 앞에 선 손님이 고개를 갸웃. 실제 상호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your team is tired of the same look.
body: You run a small café. For three years you've used the same tagline, the same green sign and the same warm, chatty tone on your menus.
Your staff say it feels stale. What do you do?

options.text: Refresh everything: new tagline, new colors, new tone
options.feedback: It feels exciting inside the café. But customers who were just starting to remember you now have to learn you again.

options.text: Keep the promise, sign and tone. Change the seasonal specials and window displays
options.feedback: You give the team and customers something new without erasing what people already remember. That's the balance this lesson is about.
You protect what people recognize. But with no new reasons to visit, consistency can slide into neglect.

cards.title: Each relaunch erased the last one.
body: Back at the bistro, each new look was well made. That wasn't the problem.
A customer who came twice a year saw a different place almost every visit. One spring it was rustic, the next it was sleek. Nothing had time to stick.
The owner thought she was adding to her brand. In fact she kept **starting over**, and paying for a new sign each time.

cards.title: Brand consistency over time
body: **Brand consistency over time** means showing customers the same core promise, look and voice for years, so each contact adds to what they already remember.
A brand lives in customers' memory, not in your files. Memory builds slowly, through repetition. Every change of message or style asks people to drop what they learned and begin again.

cards.title: You see your brand every day. Customers don't.
body: You look at your sign, menu and website daily. You hear your slogan in every meeting. Of course it feels old.
A customer might notice you a handful of times a year, often while thinking about something else. To them, your brand is barely familiar yet.
So the moment you feel bored is often the moment customers are finally starting to recognize you.

image.label: Two timelines: many owner exposures, few customer exposures
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 두 줄. 윗줄 "You"에는 점이 빽빽하게 촘촘히, 아랫줄 "Your customer"에는 점이 드문드문 몇 개만. 아랫줄 끝에 작은 전구 아이콘으로 '이제 막 기억함'을 표현.

cards.title: Same words, decades of memory.
body: De Beers has used the line "A Diamond Is Forever" since the late 1940s. Advertising Age named it the slogan of the century in 1999.
The ads around it changed many times: new photos, new couples, new media. The core promise stayed put.
That's the pattern to copy. **Keep the core steady, refresh the surface.** New campaigns can say the same thing in fresh ways.

image.label: One fixed line with changing ad frames around it
image.brief: 가운데 고정된 한 줄 문장(글자는 흐리게 처리), 주변을 시대별로 다른 스타일의 광고 액자 4개가 둘러쌈. 흑백 사진, 컬러 잡지, TV, 휴대폰 화면. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Consistent is not the same as frozen.
body: Consistency only helps if the promise is worth keeping. Repeating a promise you don't deliver just teaches customers not to trust you.
Markets also move. If your customers or your product truly change, the promise may need to change too.
When that happens, shift in small, visible steps rather than all at once. Whether and how to rebrand gets its own lesson.

cards.title: Now it's a project management app.
body: Your app's homepage has promised "Plan less, ship more" for two years, in the same blue and the same plain voice.
A new marketing lead wants to test a new headline, color scheme and tone every quarter. What do you agree to?

options.text: Test anything that might lift sign-ups, including the headline and colors
options.feedback: You may win small conversion gains each quarter. But returning users and word of mouth lose a stable picture of what you stand for.

options.text: Keep the promise, color and voice fixed. Test examples, screenshots and calls to action
options.feedback: You still learn from experiments, but inside a frame people recognize. Each test builds on the brand instead of replacing it.

options.text: Ban testing on the homepage entirely
options.feedback: The brand stays steady, but you give up useful learning about what makes the promise land.

cards.title: Change the surface, keep the core.
body: A brand is built by repetition in customers' memory. Your boredom is not a signal that customers are bored.
**Try it today:** write down your promise, your main color and your tone of voice. Check your last three ads, posts or menus. Do they all match?
